chapter: Hampton and Basie: tours and road life
title: Segregation on the road with Basie
summary: Black musicians knocking on doors for rooms at 3 a.m., sleeping on the bus, and restaurants raising prices.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Oh, I don't know. Any man that goes out on the road, unless he's going out first-class, he's making a sacrifice on his life, because if he can't do anything first-class, it's not worth having and to experience some of the things that a black musician had to experience when I was out there on the road, it was pretty tough to stomach. You would have to get off of a bus, when you come into town, three o'clock in the morning, and go around and start knocking on peoples' doors trying to find a place to stay because you couldn't stay in a white hotel and there wasn't any black hotels in the towns.
The band didn't make any kind of arrangements (inaudible) --
No, no, some -- no, no, no. Sometimes,
in certain towns, when you went in, the towns are so small that you didn't even know anybody there except the guy that was booking the engagement. You wouldn't know anyone.
Very little. Very little anything. Everybody's on their own.
You mean nobody found accommodations for the band?

No, we'd get off in little towns and there was noplace for us. In later years, it was different, after the enactment of certain freedom rights, bills that they had stuffed down peoples' throats, and after the Freedom Riders and the freedom walkers and the freedom dyers and all of those things came to pass, then you could go into a city and know that you had a reputable hotel that you could stay in and sleep and know that you could have a place where you could go in and get yourself a decent meal at almost any hour of the day. But there was noplace for you to stay. Sometimes you slept on the bus.

The bus would pull up and pull up in front of the dance hall where you were playing, and you would sleep there until daybreak, until the restaurant would open up, get yourself some breakfast and then you'd start walking up and down the streets, trying to find somebody that would take in a roomer for
that day, where you could go and sleep for the rest of that afternoon, and go to work that night and get on a bus that night and go to the next town. It was rough.

Nothing to do. You'd go into a restaurant in one of those towns and the waitress would say, "Here comes one of those bands," and they would take the menu off the table and put another menu down for you with a raise of prices. That sounds like a stage joke, and that's the truth.
